title_en: Comparison of a King and a Monk
author: John Chrysostom
occasion: The author sees most people admiring apparent goods such as wealth, power, and royal glory while despising the monastic life, so he compares the two in order to teach readers what is truly worth pursuing.
argument: Chrysostom argues that the monk who rules his passions and serves God is more truly a king than one who wears a crown and commands nations. He contrasts the king's wars, burdens, and fears with the monk's spiritual warfare, prayer, and freedom, showing that the monk's way of life is both easier to attain and more secure. Even good kings fall short of the monk's virtue, and in the future judgment the faithful monk will receive greater honor. Therefore readers should not admire the rich and powerful, but should imitate the humble, gentle monk.

outline.move: Chrysostom introduces the comparison between apparent goods such as royal power and wealth and the true goods of the monastic life, and begins contrasting what a king rules with what a monk rules.
He argues that the one who rules his passions is the true king, contrasts the monk's spiritual warfare with the king's wars, and contrasts their daily company and nightly activities.
He compares the monk's simple food, clothing, and table companions with the king's luxury, and contrasts the harm kings do through taxation and war with the monk's help to rich and poor alike.
He shows that even kings flee to holy monks and prophets in times of danger, and contrasts how a monk and a king recover after a fall and face death.
He contrasts the king's fear of assassination with the monk's security, looks ahead to the future judgment, and closes by urging readers not to admire the rich but to imitate the monk.

cast.name: John Chrysostom
cast.who: The author, writing as a Christian teacher to persuade readers to value the monastic life.

cast.name: Ahab
cast.who: King of Israel who relied on Elijah's prayers during famine.

cast.name: Elijah
cast.who: Prophet whose prayers were the hope of salvation for King Ahab.

cast.name: Hezekiah
cast.who: King of Judah who fled to the prophet Isaiah in illness and relied on Isaiah's prayers against the enemy army.

cast.name: Elisha
cast.who: Prophet to whose prayers the kings of Israel fled in war.

cast.name: Isaiah
cast.who: Prophet whose prayers Hezekiah set against the enemy army.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: Apostle whose wisdom adorns the monk's soul.

cast.name: Moses
cast.who: Lawgiver and prophet with whom the monk converses through Scripture.

cast.name: John
cast.who: A biblical author with whom the monk converses through Scripture.

key_terms.sense: The Christian monastic way of life, understood as the true philosophy of living according to Christ
The solitary or monastic life devoted to the service of God
Worldly power and lordship, especially royal authority
Kingship or royal rule, used both for earthly kingship and the kingdom of heaven
The disordered passions of the soul, such as anger, envy, greed, and pleasure, which the monk rules
Prayer, especially the monk's powerful weapon against demons and source of help for others
Demons, the spiritual enemies the monk fights and defeats
Self-control and soundness of mind, the crown the true king must possess
Piety or devotion to God, the cause for which the monk fights and may die
Christ's love for humanity, the ground of the good things described

scripture: The author uses Septuagint book names and Greek forms of biblical names. He quotes the saying 'The kingdom of heaven is within you' (Ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν ἐντὸς ὑμῶν ἐστι), which corresponds to the Gospel saying about the kingdom of God being within you (Luke 17:21). Biblical persons should be cited by their standard modern English names: Ahab, Elijah, Elisha, Isaiah, Hezekiah, Moses, Paul, John.
uncertain: The precise date of composition is not established from the text.
The original addressee is not stated in the text.
The identity of the 'John' mentioned among the biblical authors is not specified beyond the name.
Whether the enemy army in the Hezekiah episode is Assyrian or Persian is not clear from the source, which says 'Persian'.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: οὐκ Ἐζεκίας τὴν αὐτὴν ἔχων ἀρχὴν καὶ δυναστείαν, νοσῶν καὶ μέλλων τελευτᾷν, ἐφεστηκότα τὸν θάνατον ὁρῶν, ἐπὶ τὸν προφήτην κατέφυγεν, ὡς θανάτου δυνατώτερον καὶ ζωῆς χορηγόν;
_unresolved_facts.fix: Hezekiah... King of Judah who fled to the prophet in illness (death), not specifically named as Isaiah in this passage; later the text says he relied on Isaiah's prayers against the Persian enemy army

_unresolved_facts.claim: Hezekiah... relied on Isaiah's prayers against the enemy army
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Τὸ δὲ αὐτὸ τοῦτο καὶ Ἐζεκίας, τοῦ Περσικοῦ πολέμου συστάντος... τὰς Ἡσαΐου προσευχὰς ὁ βασιλεὺς ἀντέστησε ταῖς πολλαῖς τῶν Περσῶν μυριάσι
_unresolved_facts.fix: Hezekiah... King of Judah who relied on Isaiah's prayers against the Persian enemy army (the text explicitly says 'Persian' not Assyrian)

_unresolved_facts.claim: Scripture (unnamed)... Introduced by φησί, 'it says'... sections: [4, 5]
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἡ βασιλεία γὰρ, φησὶ, τῶν οὐρανῶν ἐντὸς ὑμῶν ἐστι... Αἰτεῖτε γὰρ, φησὶ, καὶ δοθήσεται ὑμῖν
_unresolved_facts.fix: Scripture (unnamed)... Introduced by φησί, 'it says'... sections: [4, 5] — but note both instances are in section 4, not section 5; section 5 contains no φησί quotation

_unresolved_facts.claim: Ἰωάννης: John — 'A biblical author with whom the monk converses through Scripture'
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text does not specify which John; could be John the Evangelist, John the Baptist, or another biblical John

_unresolved_facts.claim: Whether the enemy army in the Hezekiah episode is Assyrian or Persian is not clear from the source, which says 'Persian'
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source explicitly says 'Persian' (Περσικοῦ), which is historically anachronistic (the biblical account has Assyrians), but the source text is clear in saying Persian
